opus-5.5.text:
I think detours are almost unavoidable when you're building something at the frontier, because nobody hands you a map. Looking back on the past year, some of the things we tried were genuinely wrong turns, and I don't want to dress them up as secretly brilliant. But I also think the value of a detour depends on whether you actually learn from it, or just move on and repeat it in a different form.

One lesson for me is about focus. When you have resources and momentum, it's very tempting to do many things at once: more products, more directions, more markets. Each one looks reasonable on its own. But for a company like ours, the core question is whether we're pushing the capability of the model forward. If something doesn't serve that, it eventually becomes a distraction, even if it looks good on a growth chart for a while. I think we spread ourselves a bit thinner than we should have at certain points, and pulling back to concentrate on the fundamentals, the base model, reasoning, long-context and agentic capabilities, was one of the more important corrections we made.

The second lesson is about separating signal from noise. In this industry there's an enormous amount of external pressure: what competitors are doing, what investors expect, what the market is excited about this month. Some of our detours came from reacting to that noise rather than to our own technical judgment. Over time I've come to believe you need a kind of stubbornness. Not ignoring the world, but having a clear view of what you think AGI requires and holding yourself to that, even when it's not the popular narrative.

And third, I think detours teach you about organization, not just strategy. The way a team is structured, how decisions get made, how quickly you can kill something that isn't working: those things matter as much as any single technical bet. A lot of what we learned this year was really about how to make the organization itself more efficient at exploring and then converging.

So overall, I don't regret the detours, but I don't romanticize them either. The goal is to make each one cheaper and shorter than the last. If you can do that, then the path still bends, but it bends toward where you actually want to go.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of them as detours anymore, even though at the time some of them felt like mistakes. Looking back, the biggest one was probably getting pulled into user growth too early. We spent real resources on marketing, on acquiring users, on things that look good on a dashboard, and that's a very natural trap because everyone around you is doing it and the numbers give you a sense of momentum. But for a company like ours, the only thing that actually compounds is the model itself. If the model is a generation behind, no amount of acquisition fixes that. If the model is genuinely better, people find it on their own. So we made the decision to pull back, be more focused, and put almost everything into training and research. That was painful. It meant saying no to things, it meant some people leaving, it meant watching others grab headlines while we were quiet.

The other lesson was about how we chose what to work on. In the early period we were somewhat reactive. A competitor would release something, and we'd feel pressure to respond in that same direction. That's a mistake because you end up on someone else's roadmap. What I've come to believe is that the real differentiation comes from the thing you think is obviously important that others haven't prioritized yet. Long context was one of those for us at the start. Later it was agentic capability, the model actually doing long tasks rather than just chatting. Betting on those requires a certain tolerance for looking wrong for a while.

I also underestimated how much organizational focus matters. A small team with one clear objective moves far faster than a bigger team split across five priorities. So the "detour" wasn't just strategic, it was about rediscovering that we are at our best when we behave like a research lab with product instincts, not like an internet company that happens to have a model.

If I summarize it, I'd say the past year taught me that in this field, the courage to be boring and concentrated is undervalued. The noise is constant. The temptation to chase is constant. The companies that endure are the ones that keep returning to the fundamental question: is our model getting meaningfully better, and are we building toward where intelligence is going rather than where the market is right now.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between a detour and an experiment that didn’t work. When you’re building a company, you’re making decisions with incomplete information. Some things you can only learn by trying them, so an outcome that disappoints you doesn’t necessarily mean the decision was wrong.

The more useful question is whether we could have learned the same thing faster, with fewer resources. Did we have a clear hypothesis? Did we recognize when the evidence had changed? Or did we keep going because we’d already invested in that direction?

So I wouldn’t say the goal is to avoid every detour. It’s to shorten the feedback loop and become clearer about what really matters. At the same time, you can’t call every mistake valuable learning. The learning has to change what you do next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between detours that teach you something and detours that come from not being clear about your priorities. When you’re working with a technology that’s changing quickly, you can’t know the right path in advance. You have to try things, and some of those attempts won’t work.

But uncertainty can also become an excuse. Looking back, I’d ask: What were we trying to learn? Could we have learned it faster? And once we had enough evidence, did we make a decision, or did we keep going out of inertia?

So I wouldn’t say every detour was necessary. Some mistakes are avoidable. What matters is whether those experiences make us clearer about where to focus and quicker to recognize when an assumption is wrong.
